answer: CPR is for cardiac arrest, when the heart has stopped beating effectively. If you find someone unresponsive: call for help immediately, put them on their back, check for a pulse, open the airway and check whether they are breathing.

How to check for a pulse: feel the side of the neck nearest to you. Gently place the tips of your index and middle fingers alongside the Adam's apple. Do not use your thumb: you may confuse the beat of your own pulse with the person's. Check quickly: without a pulse the person will die unless it is quickly restored.

If the person is very cold (hypothermia, or pulled from cold water): look for breathing and feel for a pulse for at least a full minute before deciding. Breathing and pulse can be very slow and hard to detect. Do not begin chest compressions if there is any pulse, even a very slow one: that could cause a dangerous abnormal heart rhythm.

Act on what you find. No pulse: start CPR at once, chest compressions with rescue breaths, as in the steps that follow. A pulse, but not breathing or only gasping: give rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions, about one breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10 to 12 breaths a minute), until help arrives or the person starts breathing on their own; keep re-checking the pulse, and start CPR if it is lost. A pulse and breathing: place the person on their side (recovery position) and keep watching them.
Make sure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface such as the ground. Kneel beside their chest.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, between the nipples.
Press down firmly and smoothly. For an adult, compress the chest at least 2 inches (5 centimeters) deep.
Compress at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute, about 2 per second.
Let the chest fully recoil between compressions, without lifting your hands off the chest.
If you are alone, do cycles of 30 chest compressions then 2 rescue breaths. With 2 rescuers the ratio can be 30:2, or continuous compressions while the other rescuer gives the breaths.

Rescue breath: tilt the head back slightly and lift the chin, gently remove any visible obstruction from the mouth, pinch the nose closed, seal your mouth over theirs and blow for about 1 second, enough to make the chest visibly rise.

If an AED (automated external defibrillator) is available and the person has no pulse: attach it and activate it according to its operating procedures (HHS crew first-aid standard). After drowning, the JTS guideline says not to attach an AED if that delays or interferes with compressions and breaths.

Continue until professional medical help takes over or the person shows obvious signs of life: breathing normally, coughing or moving. If you become too exhausted to continue effectively, switch with another trained person.

Drowning: if the person is unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then go on as above. No pulse: cycles of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths. A pulse: rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions. The JTS drowning guideline says drowning patients whose circulation has not stopped will often respond to rescue breaths alone, and that absence of a pulse necessitates starting basic life support (CPR).
warnings: In combat casualties, cardiac arrest is nearly always the result of hemorrhagic or obstructive shock, neither of which will respond to standard CPR.
This is a general overview. Proper CPR training is needed for accurate and effective CPR.
The depth and hand placement here are for adults. Technique and the ratio of rescue breaths may vary for a child or infant.

quotes.text: In scenarios where a casualty is found already unresponsive, the procedure slightly differs: • Quickly assess the situation to understand the context and severity. • Call for immediate assistance. • Position the casualty on their back to manage and secure the airway effectively. • Check for a pulse to determine the urgency of cardiovascular support. • Open the airway using recommended techniques. • Confirm if the casualty is not breathing and, if so, proceed to attempt rescue breathing

The common points for checking the pulse are at the— • Side of the neck (carotid). • Groin (femoral). • Wrist (radial). • Ankle (posterior tibial). Note. DO NOT use your thumb to check a casualty's pulse because you may confuse the beat of your own pulse with that of the casualty. WARNING It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if the casualty has a pulse (heartbeat). Absence of a pulse (heartbeat) will lead to the death of the casualty if not quickly restored.

To ascertain the carotid pulse, locate the pulse on the casualty's neck nearest to you. Gently place the tips of your first two fingers alongside their thyroid cartilage, commonly referred to as the Adam's apple (see figure 4-1).

Depending on the casualty and their injuries, the first responder and CLS can check the casualty's pulse at the carotid artery (neck) or radial artery (wrist). The first responder and CLS should use their index and middle fingers, NOT their thumb, to check pulses (figure 15-1 on page 152).

The treatment of all near-drowning cases involves the careful removal of the victim from the water (taking care to protect the neck in the event of spinal injury), assessment for breathing and pulse (check for a full minute, if the victim has been in cold water), clearing the airway of any water, vomit or other objects), CPR, administration of oxygen, and defibrillation if necessary when appropriately trained medical personnel and equipment are available.

If the victim is in cardiopulmonary arrest (for severely hypothermic patients, check the pulse for 60 seconds before diagnosing pulselessness) CPR and modified techniques of Advance Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) must be instituted.

Signs of breathing or cardiac activity (and/or respiratory and pulse rate) should be sought for at least 1 minute because respiratory rates may be as low as 3-4 breaths per minute, pulse rates as low as 10-15 beats per minute, and pulse volume low and breaths shallow.

Check the ABCs, or the airway, breathing, and circulation of the patient. It may be difficult to detect a pulse. See current recommendations. Hypothermic patients have very slow pulses and slow shallow breathing. Do not begin chest compressions if the patient has any heart beat or pulse, even if it is very slow. This could cause dangerous abnormal heart rhythms and further complications.

In unresponsive patients, it is essential to assess peripheral pulses. Although these pulses are very difficult to detect, they must be determined before cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is initiated. Even slow heart rates may provide enough blood for the low metabolic demand of the patient. If CPR is initiated in a hypothermic person with a pulse, chest compressions could convert sinus bradycardia into a ventricular arrhythmia.

i. after performing 1 minute CPR, reassess breathing and pulse; j. if no pulse or breathing, continue CPR; k. if pulse but no breathing, continue rescue breathing; and l. if pulse and breathing present, place victim in recovery position (on side).

Assess and manage airway and provide bag-mask-ventilation (BVM) for any patient who is not breathing or not breathing adequately (too slow for age or too shallow); any unconscious patient with abnormal (slow, shallow, gasping or noisy) breathing; or any patient with a pulse who is not breathing. For patients without a pulse, follow relevant CPR protocols.

If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing and seek medical aid. If the casualty resumes breathing at any time during this procedure, the airway is kept open, and the casualty is continued to be watched.
Rescue breathing, also known as artificial ventilation, is a technique used in CPR to provide oxygen to a person who is not breathing or has inadequate breathing.
Breathing Rate: Provide rescue breaths at a rate of about one breath every five to six seconds (10 to 12 breaths per minute).
Continue Until Help Arrives: Perform rescue breathing until professional medical help arrives or until the person starts breathing on their own.
If the casualty is unconscious but breathing, the casualty should be placed in the recovery position

CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively. A general outline of the steps involved in conducting external chest compressions is: • Position: Ensure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface, such as the ground or a CPR board. Kneel beside the person's chest.

Hand Placement: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest, between the nipples. For infants or children, use two or three fingers instead of the entire hand. • Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two inches (five centimeters) deep.

Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This equates to about two compressions per second. • Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood. • Compression to Ventilation Ratio: If you are performing CPR alone, do cycles of 30 chest compressions to two rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask). If there are two rescuers, the ratio can be 30:2 or continuous chest compressions with ventilation being delivered by the other rescuer. • Continue until Help Arrives: Keep performing chest compressions until professional medical help arrives, or until the person shows signs of movement or starts breathing.

In general, CPR should be continued until one of the following conditions is met: • Signs of Life: If the person shows obvious signs of life, such as breathing normally, coughing, or moving, CPR can be stopped. • Professional Medical Help Arrives: CPR should be continued until professional medical personnel take over the resuscitation efforts. • Provider Fatigue: If the person performing CPR becomes too exhausted to continue effectively, they can switch with another trained individual to maintain the quality of compression.

Position: Ensure the casualty is lying on a flat surface, preferably with their head tilted back slightly to open the airway. • Clear the Airway: Check for any visible obstructions in the person's mouth or throat, and if present, gently remove them if possible. • Seal the Mouth: If the casualty's mouth is open, use your hand to gently lift the chin upward to maintain an open airway. With your other hand, pinch the person's nose closed to prevent air from escaping. • Breathing Technique: Place your mouth over the casualty's mouth, forming a seal, and blow into their mouth while watching for the chest to rise. Deliver the breath over one second and make sure it is sufficient to visibly inflate the chest.

In a graded practical exercise, given an adult manikin designed for cardio-pulmonary resuscitation, simulating a patient in pulseless V-tach, Vtach over the maximum rate, or V-fib, and an Automated External Defibrillator (AED),

The candidate correctly demonstrates, according to standards of the American Heart Association: a. attaching AED to pulseless victim over 12 years-of-age and 90 pounds; b. activating AED according to operating procedures; and

Most common dysrhythmias are asystole and pulseless electrical activity. Defibrillation is not indicated with these rhythms. Attempts to attach an AED should not be made if it delays or interferes with compressions and ventilation.

It is important to note that these steps provide a general overview of external chest compressions. Proper CPR training and certification are needed to gain a thorough understanding of the technique and to ensure accurate and effective application during emergency situations.

External chest compressions, also known as Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), in combat casualties is nearly always the result of hemorrhagic or obstructive shock, neither of which will respond to standard CPR. Conducting CPR may delay definitive treatment in nearly all cases.

It is important to note that the technique and ratio of rescue breaths may vary depending on the age of the person receiving CPR (such as an adult, child, or infant) and the specific guidelines in the area or operation.

If unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with traditional basic life support utilizing a ratio of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths. Five breaths are used initially as a recruitment maneuver. Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone.
While pulses may be difficult to identify due to hypothermia or hypotension, absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support/Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols.

conflict: CPR NUMBERS (the card shows the 2026 values): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says 30 compressions to 2 breaths, 100 to 120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) agrees (30 compressions, at least 2 inches, at least 100 per minute, 2 rescue breaths). HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 (crew training assessment standard, older guidelines) says cycles of 15 compressions to 2 ventilations (5 to 1 with two rescuers), 80 to 100 compressions per minute, depth 1½ to 2 inches, hands two finger widths above the tip of the breastbone, each breath taking 1½ to 2 seconds, and a carotid pulse check of 5 to 10 seconds. Owner to confirm the newer Army values stand. WHO-ICRC BEC 2018 gives no CPR method ('follow relevant CPR protocols'); FEMA P-2064 (2020) only says to take CPR training. Note also ATP 4-02.11 para 6-44: CPR on combat trauma casualties 'should be a rare circumstance'. WHAT TO DO AFTER THE CHECKS (lines added in revision): the rule is stated outright by the HHS 2003 crew standard ('if no pulse or breathing, continue CPR; if pulse but no breathing, continue rescue breathing; if pulse and breathing present, place victim in recovery position') and by WHO BEC (ventilate 'any patient with a pulse who is not breathing'; 'For patients without a pulse, follow relevant CPR protocols'). ATP 4-02.11 has the pieces but not the rule in one place: para 5-37 check for a pulse, para 6-15 'If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing', para 6-45 compressions for cardiac arrest, para 6-49 one rescue breath every five to six seconds. No disagreement found. 'Or only gasping' follows WHO BEC, which ventilates an unconscious patient with 'abnormal (slow, shallow, gasping or noisy) breathing'. The re-check of the pulse comes from the HHS standard, which re-assesses after 1 minute of its older 15:2 CPR; the card gives no interval. The HHS decision quote comes from the same older standard as the 15:2 numbers above. COLD PERSON: HHS says check breathing and pulse 'for a full minute' after cold water and the pulse 'for 60 seconds' in severe hypothermia; TB MED 508 (2026) says 'at least 1 minute'; TC 21-3 (2025) says to breathe for a severely hypothermic casualty for 3 to 15 minutes before moving them (not in this card). AED: the only instruction in the kit on using an AED is the HHS 2003 crew standard ('attaching AED to pulseless victim over 12 years-of-age and 90 pounds', 'activating AED according to operating procedures'); the CPR sections of ATP 4-02.11 (2026) and ATP 3-50.21 (2018) do not mention AEDs; JTS Drowning 2025 says AEDs have a limited role in drowning (shockable rhythms in less than 6% of patients) and must not delay or interfere with compressions and ventilation; TB MED 507 (2022) mentions automated defibrillation only as part of advanced life support during transport. The words 'over 12 years-of-age and 90 pounds' describe the victim in that 2003 graded manikin exercise; they are not a rule for when an AED may be used, and they are outdated. After the re-review they are no longer in the answer line: shown on the phone, with no child card, they could stop someone using an AED on an older child (the reviewer notes, from outside the kit, that current resuscitation practice uses AEDs on children, with child pads where available). The words still appear in the HHS quote, which is the only kit source for the AED line and is quoted whole. PULSE CHECK (line added after the re-review, on the reviewer's recommendation): because the card withholds chest compressions when a pulse is felt, a mistaken pulse is the main way it can harm. How to feel for the pulse is ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 4-21 (common points: side of the neck, groin, wrist, ankle; 'DO NOT use your thumb'), para 4-23 (carotid pulse: on the casualty's neck nearest to you, tips of the first two fingers alongside the Adam's apple) and para 15-6 (neck or wrist; index and middle fingers, NOT the thumb). The card names the neck only: the same manual notes that the absence of a wrist (radial) pulse is a sign of shock, so a missing wrist pulse does not show that the heart has stopped. How long to feel: ATP 4-02.11 gives no time, but the warning box in para 4-21 says 'It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if the casualty has a pulse (heartbeat)', which the card gives as 'Check quickly'; the HHS 2003 crew standard, a manikin test, has the candidate check the carotid pulse 'for 5 to 10 seconds' (not on the card; the owner may want it shown, attributed); the only time on the card is the full minute for a cold person. The kit has no rule for a pulse the rescuer is not sure of. For the owner, from outside the kit (reviewer's note): current lay-rescuer guidance skips the pulse check. DROWNING (last line, changed after the re-review): JTS Drowning 2025 says, in one paragraph, 'begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with traditional basic life support utilizing a ratio of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths' and 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone', and under Circulation 'absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support/Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols'. The earlier wording told the reader to compress after the 5 breaths whatever the pulse, which contradicted the card's own rule (a pulse but not breathing: rescue breaths only); the line now gives compressions only when there is no pulse. No kit source disagrees. The reviewed card drowning-rescue-care still has the earlier, unconditional wording ('begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with 30 chest compressions and 2 rescue breaths, repeated'); it was not part of this revision.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Pass. Previous findings fixed: (1) A14 (drowning) now gives 30:2 only with no pulse and rescue breaths only with a pulse, attributed to JTS Drowning 2025 (Initial Resuscitation: 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone'; Circulation: 'absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support'), and its 'go on as above' brings in A4's re-check; it no longer contradicts A4. (2) The AED line no longer carries 'over 12 years of age and 90 pounds' (kept in conflict and in the whole HHS quote); 'attach it and activate it according to its operating procedures' is attributed to the HHS crew standard and the drowning limit to JTS. (3) The recommended pulse-check line A2 is added and faithful to ATP 4-02.11 4-21 (common points, 'DO NOT use your thumb', the 'quickly determine' warning), 4-23 (neck nearest you, fingertips alongside the Adam's apple) and 15-6 (index and middle fingers). Pulse rule checked across the linked cards: cpr-adult, drowning-rescue-care, burn-first-aid and choking-adult all say no pulse: compressions; a pulse but not breathing: rescue breaths only; all three pointers use this card's exact title, 'CPR for an adult'. (Only this card also says to keep re-checking the pulse during rescue breaths; the drowning and choking cards are sent back to add it.) JTS Table 2 ('When to initiate: Patient with respiratory distress or respiratory arrest'): it need not be shown on the phone, because it is not a disagreement. The Circulation paragraph sends the reader to Table 2 from its 'absence of a pulse' sentence; Initial Resuscitation says patients without circulatory arrest often respond to breaths alone; Table 3 grades 'Apnea +Pulse' (grade 5) apart from 'Apnea without Pulse' (grade 6); and read literally Table 2 would start compressions on a breathing patient in respiratory distress, which no kit source supports. Everything else unchanged and still faithful; kind protocol; all asks answered (including 'has a pulse but is not breathing'); no PDF junk. Optional: (a) the conflict field is stale: it says drowning-rescue-care 'still has the earlier, unconditional wording', but commit 9067a45 changed that card to this card's pulse rule; replace the sentence so the owner's record is right; (b) add one sentence to the DROWNING note on JTS Table 2 and Table 3, as recorded on drowning-rescue-care, so both cards carry the same record; (c) A14 (drowning: 5 rescue breaths first) comes after the 30:2 steps; placing it right after A4 would put it before a rescuer starts compressions. Owner note carried forward: the pulse-based rule follows the kit; current lay-rescuer guidance (outside the kit) skips the pulse check, and a mistaken pulse is the main way this card can harm. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Previous findings fixed: A3 gives the decision rule (no pulse: CPR; pulse but not breathing or only gasping: rescue breaths only, one every 5-6 s, re-check the pulse; pulse and breathing: recovery position) and A2 the full-minute check in a cold person (HHS, TB MED 508). A3 needs no attribution: the HHS 2003 crew standard (items i-l) and WHO BEC state the rule, ATP 4-02.11 has every part (5-37, 6-15, 6-45, 6-49), ATP 3-50.21 gives no rule, JTS Drowning supports it, and no kit source disagrees; 'only gasping' rests on WHO BEC. Remaining problems: (1) A13 now contradicts A3. 'Drowning: ... begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths' tells the reader to compress a drowned person even with a pulse, and drowning is the commonest case of a pulse without breathing. The same JTS paragraph says 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone', and its Circulation section says 'absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support/Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols'. Fix: 'Drowning: if unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then go on as above: no pulse, 30 compressions and 2 breaths; a drowned person who still has a pulse often responds to rescue breaths alone (JTS).' (2) AED line: the 2003 HHS standard is an acceptable source for 'attach it to a person with no pulse and use it according to its instructions', and the JTS drowning limit is correctly attributed, but the clause 'which specifies a victim over 12 years of age and 90 pounds' is the setting of a USCG/STCW manikin exercise, not a usage rule, and it is outdated (current resuscitation practice uses AEDs on children, with child pads where available). Shown on the phone, with no child card, it can stop someone using an AED on an older child. Fix: drop that clause from the answer (keep it in conflict). Recommended: since A3 now withholds compressions when a pulse is felt, a mistaken pulse is the main way this card can harm; add how to feel for it from ATP 4-02.11 4-21 and 15-6 (side of the neck, index and middle fingers; 'DO NOT use your thumb to check a casualty's pulse because you may confuse the beat of your own pulse with that of the casualty'). The kit has no rule for an uncertain pulse; owner to note that current lay-rescuer guidance skips the pulse check. Everything else checked against its quote; kind protocol correct; asks answered; no PDF junk. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Problem: no decision rule after the checks. A1 says to check for a pulse and breathing, then the card goes straight to compressions; it never says what each result means. ATP 4-02.11 6-15: 'If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing and seek medical aid', and 6-49 describes rescue breathing for a person who is not breathing; compressions are for 'cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively'. A reader with a person who has a pulse but is not breathing (overdose, drowning, lightning) is not told to give rescue breaths only, and may compress a beating heart (the hypothermia card warns this can cause a fatal rhythm). Fix: 'No pulse and not breathing normally: start chest compressions (30:2). Pulse present but not breathing: give rescue breaths only and keep checking the pulse.' Add: in a very cold person, feel for the pulse for a full minute first (TB MED 508, HHS). Confirmed: ATP 4-02.11 5-37, 6-45 (position, hand placement, 2 in depth, 100-120/min, full recoil, 30:2, when to stop), 6-49 rescue-breath technique, 6-44 combat note, training caveat; JTS 5 initial breaths for drowning. HHS's older 15:2 numbers are listed in conflict. No PDF junk. Recommended: HHS's crew standard includes attaching an AED to a pulseless victim; 'if an AED is available, attach it and follow its prompts' is worth adding.
